summary.text: An explicit check at \(n=10\) and an inductively preserved head–tail invariant for the first three iterated run-length encodings yield eventual recurrences \(k_{n+1}=k_n+q_n\), \(q_{n+1}=q_n+p_n\), and \(p_{n+5}=p_{n+4}+k_n\), while row length and row sum are successive partial sums of the run count \(k_n\). For the root \(\rho\in(1,2)\) of \(\rho^4(\rho-1)^3=1\), a positive left-eigenvector potential grows exactly by \(\rho\); comparison bounds transfer \(\Theta(\rho^n)\) growth through those partial sums, so squeezing the \(n\)-th roots gives convergence to \(\rho\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rl}(w)\) denote the word of lengths of the maximal constant runs of a finite word \(w\). Thus, for example,
\[
 \operatorname{rl}(2,1,1,1,3,1)=(1,3,1,1).
\]
Let \(T_n\) be the rows in the definition of A381587, indexed as in the question, and put
\[
 U_n=\operatorname{rev}(T_n).
\]
Reversing the defining recurrence for the rows gives, for every \(n\geq 3\),
\[
 U_{n+1}=U_n\,\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{rl}(U_n)). \tag{1}
\]
Here and below juxtaposition denotes concatenation. The desired number \(a(n)\) is the sum of the entries of \(U_n\), since reversal does not change a sum.

We will first establish sufficiently precise recurrences for several statistics of these words. The main point is to control the possible merger of the two runs at a concatenation boundary.

For a word \(w\), write
\[
 \mathcal R(w)=((v_1,c_1),\ldots,(v_r,c_r))
\]
for its run encoding: \(w\) consists of \(c_1\) copies of \(v_1\), then \(c_2\) copies of \(v_2\), and so on. Thus every \(c_i>0\), adjacent \(v_i\)'s are different, and
\[
 \operatorname{rl}(w)=(c_1,\ldots,c_r).
\]
The following elementary facts about run encodings will be used repeatedly.

1. Decoding \(\mathcal R(w)\) recovers \(w\).

2. Reversal commutes with run encoding:
\[
 \mathcal R(\operatorname{rev}w)=\operatorname{rev}(\mathcal R(w)). \tag{2}
\]
The values in the pairs are unchanged under this reversal.

3. To find \(\mathcal R(xy)\), concatenate \(\mathcal R(x)\) and \(\mathcal R(y)\), except that if the last value of \(x\) equals the first value of \(y\), the two boundary pairs \((v,c)\), \((v,d)\) are replaced by \((v,c+d)\). Consequently the number of runs is the sum of the two numbers of runs, minus one exactly when this boundary merger occurs.

4. If the last run of \(w\) is \((v,c)\), then deleting the last letter changes that final run to \((v,c-1)\) when \(c\geq2\), and removes it when \(c=1\).

All of these statements follow directly by splitting a word into its maximal constant blocks. They also show that every run list has positive counts and unequal adjacent values, so that run encoding and decoding are inverse operations on such lists.

Define
\[
 Y_n=\operatorname{rl}(U_n),\qquad
 Z_n=\operatorname{rl}(Y_n),\qquad
 W_n=\operatorname{rl}(Z_n). \tag{3}
\]
We use the following numerical statistics:
\[
 R_n=\#\mathcal R(U_n),\qquad
 A_{2,n}=\#\mathcal R(Y_n),\qquad
 A_{3,n}=\#\mathcal R(Z_n). \tag{4}
\]
Notice also that
\[
 \#\mathcal R(w)=|\operatorname{rl}(w)|. \tag{5}
\]

We now develop the structural information needed to handle all boundary mergers.

A direct computation from the initial rows gives
\[
 U_6=(2,1,1,1,3,1). \tag{6}
\]
Equation (1) says that each later \(U_n\) has the previous one as a prefix. Hence every \(U_n\), \(n\geq6\), begins
\[
 2,1,1,1,3,1. \tag{7}
\]
In particular, its run-length word begins
\[
 Y_n=1,3,1,\ldots. \tag{8}
\]
It follows from (1) and (8), by induction, that every \(U_n\), \(n\geq6\), ends in
\[
 1,3,1, \tag{9}
\]
and in particular ends in \(3,1\). Indeed (9) is true in (6); if \(Y_n=1,3,1,s\), then the appended word \(\operatorname{rev}(Y_n)\) ends in \(\operatorname{rev}(1,3,1)=(1,3,1)\). Consequently, the last run of \(U_n\) is the singleton
\[
 (1,1). \tag{10}
\]
It follows as well that \(Y_n\) ends in the symbol \(1\), and therefore the last run of \(Y_n\) has value \(1\), though its count is not yet specified.

Using (1), (2), and the boundary rule, we can already count the runs of \(U_{n+1}\). The two run lists being joined are \(\mathcal R(U_n)\) and \(\operatorname{rev}(\mathcal R(Y_n))\). By (10), the first ends in a run of value \(1\); the second begins with a run of value \(1\), because \(Y_n\) ends in \(1\). Exactly one boundary merger therefore occurs. Hence, for \(n\geq6\),
\[
 R_{n+1}+1=R_n+A_{2,n}. \tag{11}
\]

The more delicate facts needed at the next two levels are packaged in the following invariant, valid for every \(n\geq10\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(I1)}\quad&\mathcal R(Y_n)\text{ ends in }(1,6),\\
\text{(I2)}\quad&\mathcal R(Z_n)\text{ ends in }(1,3),(6,1),\\
\text{(I3)}\quad&\mathcal R(Z_n)\text{ begins }(1,6),(3,1),x
                   \text{ for some run }x,\\
\text{(I4)}\quad&W_n=6\,\operatorname{tail}(U_{n-4}).
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\]
We prove all four assertions simultaneously by induction.

For the base case \(n=10\), direct iteration of (1) from the initial rows gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathcal R(Y_{10})\text{ ends in }(1,6),\\
&\mathcal R(Z_{10})=((1,6),(3,1),(1,1),(5,1),(1,3),(6,1)),\\
&W_{10}=(6,1,1,1,3,1)=6\,\operatorname{tail}(U_6).
\end{aligned} \tag{13}
\]
These explicit run lists establish (I1)--(I4) at \(10\). We now show that the assertions propagate.

Assume (12) at some \(n\geq10\). Since the last runs of \(U_n\) and \(Y_n\) are respectively \((1,1)\) and \((1,6)\), applying the boundary rule to
\[
 U_{n+1}=U_n\operatorname{rev}(Y_n)
\]
shows that the two boundary runs merge into a run of length \(1+6=7\). Deleting the final symbol of \(Y_n\) shortens its last run from length \(6\) to length \(5\). Since run lengths of a reversed word are the reversed run lengths, we obtain
\[
 Y_{n+1}=\operatorname{dropLast}(Y_n)\,7\,
          \operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{dropLast}(Z_n)). \tag{14}
\]
Now encode (14) into runs. By (I2), deleting the last symbol of \(Z_n\) removes its final singleton run \((6,1)\); the new initial symbol \(7\) is different from the adjacent values \(1\). Thus
\[
 \mathcal R(Y_{n+1})=
 \operatorname{dropLast}(\mathcal R(Y_n))
 \,((1,5),(7,1))\,
 \operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{dropLast}(\mathcal R(Z_n))). \tag{15}
\]
No unmentioned merger occurs in (15): the displayed boundary values are \(1\) and \(7\), and (I2) says that after the terminal \((6,1)\) is removed from \(\mathcal R(Z_n)\), its last run is \((1,3)\), so the reversed list starts with value \(1\), again different from \(7\).

Taking lengths in (15), and observing that deleting the last element lowers the length by one on both nonempty run lists, gives
\[
 A_{2,n+1}=A_{2,n}+A_{3,n}. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed the left part contributes \(A_{2,n}-1\), the two displayed runs contribute \(2\), and the reversed final part contributes \(A_{3,n}-1\).

Reading only the counts in (15) gives the corresponding word identity one level higher:
\[
 Z_{n+1}=\operatorname{dropLast}(Z_n)\,5,1\,
          \operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{dropLast}(W_n)). \tag{17}
\]

We need to encode (17). From (I4), (7), and (9), the word \(W_n\) begins
\[
 6,1,1,1,3,1,\ldots \tag{18}
\]
and ends in \(1,3,1\). Hence its first three runs are
\[
 (6,1),(1,3),(3,1), \tag{19}
\]
and its last two runs are
\[
 (3,1),(1,1). \tag{20}
\]
The last statement uses that the final three symbols are pairwise unequal at the two indicated boundaries.

By (I2), deleting the last symbol from \(Z_n\) removes its final singleton run \((6,1)\). By (20), deleting the last symbol from \(W_n\) removes its final singleton run \((1,1)\). The displayed symbols \(5,1\) form singleton runs, and the surrounding values are distinct: the preceding run in \(Z_n\) has value \(1\), so it does not merge with \(5\), while after reversal the next value is \(3\), so it does not merge with the displayed \(1\). Thus
\[
 \mathcal R(Z_{n+1})=
 \operatorname{dropLast}(\mathcal R(Z_n))
 \,((5,1),(1,1))\,
 \operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{dropLast}(\mathcal R(W_n))). \tag{21}
\]

Reading the counts in (21) yields
\[
 W_{n+1}=\operatorname{dropLast}(W_n)\,1,1\,
          \operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{dropLast}(\operatorname{rl}(W_n))). \tag{22}
\]
Both \(W_n\) and \(\operatorname{rl}(W_n)\) end in the symbol \(1\), by (20). Restoring these two deleted final symbols in (22) therefore gives the simpler self-reading identity
\[
 W_{n+1}=W_n\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{rl}(W_n)). \tag{23}
\]

We can now verify all four parts of the invariant at \(n+1\).

First, by (I3), \(\operatorname{dropLast}(\mathcal R(Z_n))\) still begins with \((1,6)\): (I3) provides at least three initial runs, while only the last run is deleted. Therefore (15), whose last block is the reversal of this list, ends in \((1,6)\). This is (I1) at \(n+1\).

Second, by (19), deleting the last run of \(\mathcal R(W_n)\) leaves a list still beginning with \((6,1),(1,3)\). Its reversal therefore ends in \((1,3),(6,1)\). Equation (21) proves (I2) at \(n+1\).

Third, (I3) at \(n\) says that \(\mathcal R(Z_n)\) starts with \((1,6),(3,1)\) and has at least one further run. Deleting its last run preserves the first two; if it removes the only further run, the newly appended run \((5,1)\) supplies a third run. Thus (21) proves (I3) at \(n+1\).

Finally, we prove (I4). Since \(U_{n-4}\) begins with \(2,1\), its tail begins with \(1\). Thus (I4) implies
\[
 \operatorname{rl}(W_n)=1\,\operatorname{rl}(\operatorname{tail}(U_{n-4})).
\]
On the other hand, because the deleted first symbol of \(U_{n-4}\) is \(2\), different from the following \(1\), the right side is exactly \(Y_{n-4}=\operatorname{rl}(U_{n-4})\). Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{rl}(W_n)=Y_{n-4}. \tag{24}
\]
Using (23), (I4), (24), and then (1), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
 W_{n+1}
 &=6\,\operatorname{tail}(U_{n-4})\operatorname{rev}(Y_{n-4})\\
 &=6\,\operatorname{tail}\bigl(U_{n-4}\operatorname{rev}(Y_{n-4})\bigr)\\
 &=6\,\operatorname{tail}(U_{n-3}),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is (I4) at \(n+1\). This completes the induction and proves (12) for every \(n\geq10\).

We next translate the invariant into numerical recurrences. Let
\[
 L_n=|U_n|,
 \qquad S_n=\sum_{u\in U_n}u=a(n). \tag{25}
\]
From (1), the length of the appended word is the number of runs of \(U_n\), while the sum of its entries is the sum of the run lengths of \(U_n\), namely \(|U_n|\). Hence, for \(n\geq3\),
\[
 L_{n+1}=L_n+R_n,
 \qquad
 S_{n+1}=S_n+L_n. \tag{26}
\]

Also, by (5),
\[
 A_{3,n}=|W_n|.
\]
For \(n\geq10\), (I4) and the nonemptiness of \(U_{n-4}\) show that adjoining the initial \(6\) exactly compensates for deleting the first symbol of \(U_{n-4}\). Therefore
\[
 A_{3,n}=L_{n-4}. \tag{27}
\]
Combining (27) with the first recurrence in (26), we get, for \(n\geq10\),
\[
 A_{3,n+5}=A_{3,n+4}+R_n. \tag{28}
\]

Set
\[
 k_n=R_n,\qquad q_n=A_{2,n}-1,\qquad p_n=A_{3,n}. \tag{29}
\]
The invariant implies \(A_{2,n}\geq1\) for \(n\geq10\). Therefore (11), (16), and (28) become, for all \(n\geq10\),
\[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
 k_{n+1}&=k_n+q_n,\\
 q_{n+1}&=q_n+p_n,\\
 p_{n+5}&=p_{n+4}+k_n.
\end{aligned}} \tag{30}
\]

We will also need elementary comparisons. For every finite word, the number of runs is at most its length. Applying this successively gives
\[
 A_{3,n}\leq A_{2,n}\leq R_n. \tag{31}
\]
Indeed, \(A_{2,n}=\#\mathcal R(Y_n)\leq |Y_n|=\#\mathcal R(U_n)=R_n\), and similarly \(A_{3,n}\leq A_{2,n}\). Thus
\[
 0\leq q_n\leq k_n,
 \qquad 0\leq p_n\leq k_n. \tag{32}
\]
Moreover \(k_{10}>0\), since \(U_{10}\) is nonempty. The first equation of (30) shows that \(k_n\) is nondecreasing for \(n\geq10\).

We now analyze the growth of (30). Consider
\[
 f(x)=x^4(x-1)^3.
\]
This is continuous, with \(f(1)=0\) and \(f(2)=16\). By the intermediate value theorem there is a real number \(\rho\) satisfying
\[
 1<\rho<2,
 \qquad \rho^4(\rho-1)^3=1. \tag{33}
\]
(The inequalities are strict because neither endpoint has value \(1\).)

For \(n\geq10\), define the positive linear functional
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi_n={}&(\rho-1)^2k_{n+4}+(\rho-1)q_{n+4}+p_{n+4}\\
 &+(\rho-1)^3\bigl(k_{n+3}+\rho k_{n+2}+\rho^2k_{n+1}+\rho^3k_n\bigr).
\end{aligned} \tag{34}
\]
Substitute the three equations in (30) into \(\Psi_{n+1}\). The terms involving \(q_{n+4}\), \(p_{n+4}\), and the shifted \(k\)'s collect exactly into \(\rho\Psi_n\); the only remaining coefficient is a multiple of
\(
1-\rho^4(\rho-1)^3,
\)
which is zero by (33). Hence
\[
 \Psi_{n+1}=\rho\Psi_n \qquad(n\geq10). \tag{35}
\]
For completeness, this cancellation can be seen directly by replacing
\[
 k_{n+5}=k_{n+4}+q_{n+4},\quad
 q_{n+5}=q_{n+4}+p_{n+4},\quad
 p_{n+5}=p_{n+4}+k_n
\]
in (34), expanding, and moving \(\rho\Psi_n\) to the left; the result is
\[
 k_n\bigl(1-\rho^4(\rho-1)^3\bigr)=0.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \Psi_n=\rho^{n-10}\Psi_{10}. \tag{36}
\]
All coefficients in (34) are nonnegative, and the coefficient of \(k_{n+4}\) is positive. Since \(k_{10}>0\) and \(k\) is nondecreasing, \(\Psi_{10}>0\).

We compare \(\Psi_n\) to \(k_{n+4}\). The first term gives
\[
 (\rho-1)^2k_{n+4}\leq\Psi_n. \tag{37}
\]
On the other hand, monotonicity gives \(k_{n+j}\leq k_{n+4}\) for \(0\leq j\leq3\), and (32) gives \(q_{n+4},p_{n+4}\leq k_{n+4}\). Hence
\[
 \Psi_n\leq Dk_{n+4}, \tag{38}
\]
where the positive constant
\[
 D=(\rho-1)^2+(\rho-1)+1
   +(\rho-1)^3(1+\rho+\rho^2+\rho^3) \tag{39}
\]
is independent of \(n\). Combining (36)--(38), and merely absorbing the fixed index shift and the fixed factor \(\Psi_{10}\) into constants, yields positive constants \(c_k,C_k\) such that
\[
 c_k\rho^m\leq k_m\leq C_k\rho^m
 \qquad(m\geq14). \tag{40}
\]

It remains to transfer these estimates first to \(L_n\), then to \(S_n\). We record the elementary upper-bound principle being used. If \(b_{n+1}=b_n+d_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), if \(d_n\leq A\rho^n\), and if \(\rho>1\), then
\[
 b_n\leq C\rho^n

after increasing a positive constant \(C\). Indeed, choose \(C\) large enough to dominate the initial value and to satisfy \(A\leq C(\rho-1)\). Then
\[
 b_{n+1}\leq C\rho^n+A\rho^n
 \leq C\rho^{n+1},
\]
and induction proves the claim.

Apply this principle to \(L_{n+1}=L_n+k_n\) and the upper bound in (40). There is \(C_L>0\) such that
\[
 L_n\leq C_L\rho^n

eventually. Applying it once more to \(S_{n+1}=S_n+L_n\), there is \(C_S>0\) such that
\[
 S_n\leq C_S\rho^n

eventually. \tag{41}
\]
For lower bounds, (26) and nonnegativity give
\[
 L_n=L_{n-1}+k_{n-1}\geq k_{n-1}
      \geq (c_k/\rho)\rho^n

eventually, and then
\[
 S_n=S_{n-1}+L_{n-1}\geq L_{n-1}
      \geq (c_k/\rho^2)\rho^n

eventually. \tag{42}
\]
Thus for some constants \(c,C>0\),
\[
 c\rho^n\leq S_n\leq C\rho^n \tag{43}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).

Finally, take logarithms in (43). Since \(c>0\) and \(\rho>0\), (43) also guarantees that \(S_n>0\) eventually, and
\[
 \log c+n\log\rho\leq\log S_n
 \leq\log C+n\log\rho.
\]
After division by \(n\), both outer expressions tend to \(\log\rho\). Therefore
\[
 \frac{\log S_n}{n}\longrightarrow\log\rho.
\]
Exponentiating gives
\[
 S_n^{1/n}\longrightarrow\rho. \tag{44}
\]
Since \(S_n=a(n)=\mathrm{A381358}(n)\), this proves not only that the requested limit exists, but that it is the number \(\rho\in(1,2)\) satisfying
\[
 \boxed{\rho^4(\rho-1)^3=1}.
\]
In particular, \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a(n)^{1/n}\) exists.
